analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict their marketing, and require ingredient disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in April 2000 and never received a vote; it died when that Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written the FDA's 1996 tobacco rules into law, giving the Health and Human Services Secretary clear power to regulate cigarettes and other tobacco products as drug-delivery devices. It required manufacturers to disclose every ingredient and turn over their internal research on nicotine and addiction, restricted advertising aimed at young people, set new warning labels, and let the government restrict or eliminate mail-order cigarette sales to minors. It deliberately left tobacco farmers and warehouses alone. It never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face fewer avenues to buy cigarettes through the mail and less advertising aimed at them, plus the general public through stricter warnings, ingredient disclosure, and reduced-risk claims that must be scientifically proven before manufacturers can make them. The bill's stated purpose, in its own title, is 'protection of children from tobacco' [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act so the Secretary of Health and Human Services can regulate any tobacco product as a drug, a device, or both, and makes the FDA's 1996 tobacco rule lawful under the act [S2][S3].

Requires each manufacturer to file an annual list of every ingredient and nicotine content for each brand, submit safety assessments for new ingredients before using them, and disclose to the Secretary all nonpublic research relating to addiction, dependency, or the health and safety of tobacco products [S2][S3].

Directs the Secretary to implement the marketing, advertising, and access restrictions and the new warning-label specifications agreed to in the 1997 settlement between tobacco manufacturers and state attorneys general, and to review and restrict mail-order tobacco sales if minors are obtaining products that way [S2][S3].

Bars manufacturers from claiming a product reduces health risk unless they demonstrate to the Secretary, with scientific evidence, that it significantly reduces overall health risk, and creates a scientific advisory committee to study whether nicotine levels can exist that do not cause dependence [S2][S3].
Preserves state and local authority to impose additional tobacco-control measures beyond the federal floor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would bear the cost of ingredient testing and disclosure, turning over internal research files, good-manufacturing-practice compliance, advertising restrictions, and new warning labels. Consumers could see some of those compliance costs passed through to cigarette prices. Tobacco farmers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives are explicitly exempt from the entire act [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill adopts the restrictions from the 1997 settlement between manufacturers and state attorneys general rather than tougher independent standards, and it preempts states from requiring warning labels other than the federal ones (Sec. 572(d)), which could have limited stronger state-level labeling [S3].

It exempts tobacco leaf producers—growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives—from the entire act and bars the Secretary from regulating leaf production, carving out a politically powerful segment of the industry [S2][S3].

The bill keeps cigarettes legal for adult sale so long as they meet performance standards, and its 'best public health result' balancing test weighs risks to the whole population, meaning regulation rather than any restriction on adult access to the products themselves [S3].
Its funding has a trigger: no spending under the new authority in any year FDA appropriations fall below the prior year's level, so its programs could stall in a budget fight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong: nicotine addiction usually starts in youth, and the bill targets the main tools the industry used to reach them—advertising, weak warnings, unverified 'light' and 'reduced risk' claims, and mail-order access—while forcing disclosure of what manufacturers knew about addiction. The trade-offs are real but modest: costs passed to consumers in cigarette prices, a carve-out for tobacco farmers, and warning-label preemption that could have capped stronger state rules. On balance the bill was designed to protect the public at direct expense to manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in April 2000, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the KIDS Act on April 6, 2000, joined by original cosponsors Lincoln Chafee and Bob Graham; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S5].
It attracted four cosponsors in total (three Democrats and one Republican) [S4].

No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and no version of it passed either chamber before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers are better off: the bill that would have forced ingredient disclosure, handed regulators their internal addiction research, and restricted their marketing never advanced, leaving them to keep selling under the existing, lighter rules for the time being.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on April 6, 2000—no markup, no vote, no report before the Congress ended.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry opposed FDA jurisdiction over tobacco; in 2000 the Supreme Court ruled FDA lacked authority to regulate tobacco, the legal gap this bill was written to close.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan—a Democratic sponsor and cosponsors including one Republican—but with only five senators behind it, no floor vote ever tested either party's position.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed ingredient disclosure, turned over the companies' internal research on nicotine and addiction, applied good-manufacturing-practice standards, restricted their advertising, and required scientifically proven claims for any 'reduced risk' marketing. Those costs are the flip side of the public health protections, so the industry's interest in the bill ran against the public's.

industries.industry: Tobacco leaf farmers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts them from every provision and bars the Secretary from regulating leaf production or entering farms without written consent, shielding growers from the compliance burden falling on manufacturers.

Retailers must ensure the products they sell comply with the act, and stores accessible to minors that mainly sell tobacco must follow advertising restrictions—but retailers gain from the preemption of state warning-label rules beyond the federal ones.
